newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB's Roth sees only modest Swiss recovery in 1997.
newsitem.headline: SNB's Roth sees only modest Swiss recovery in 1997.

text.p: The Swiss economy is likely to improve in coming months, but is expected to post only modest growth in 1997, Swiss National Bank Vice-chairman Jean-Pierre Roth said.

"I completely agree with those who do not believe the recovery will manifest itself with vigour in 1997," Roth said in the text of a speech to be presented in Geneva to the Centre International d'Etudes Monetaires et Bancaires.

"Without any doubt -- we already sense this now -- the economy will recover and will continue to improve in the months ahead. There is reason to be glad, but (not yet) to cry victory. We cannot be lulled by illusion," he said.
He also said U.S. interest rates could continue to move higher following the Fed's resumption of a more restrictive monetary policy in March.
"We believe there is a big probability there will be changes in U.S. interest rates in the months ahead," Roth said.

"If Europe is pulled into the movement towards higher rates, the economic recovery is which is already fragile, will likely be compromised, or, at the very least, continue at a slower pace," he added.

"At the heart of the problem, of course, is the position of the dollar. If its firming trend continues, the conditions for a recovery remain favourable. (But) if some new problem should arise ...(this) will weigh on the European (economic) cycle, and hence also on our own country," Roth said.
The SNB, which has forecast 0.5 percent gross domestic product growth this year. has made clear it will adjust its generous monetary policy only when GDP is clearly expanding.

Roth said the start-up of Europe's single currency, the euro, set to be launched in January 1999, could create an uncertain business climate and also was likely to encourage caution in European monetary policy.

"Could one imagine -- as markets wait to see what the future quality of the euro will be -- that European monetary authorities would take the slightest risk with respect to monetary expansion? I don't think so," Roth said.
Any dollar gains amid uncertainty surrounding currency union could be positive for Europe and Switzerland, Roth said.

"But one must emphasise one positive point: the uncertainty in Europe seems mainly to benefit the dollar's advance. It is possible that the situation of the strong dollar which we have now will be maintained in the months ahead, which would also lead me to believe that the Swiss franc will not necessarily be forced into the centre of the turbulence that the process of European monetary integration could witness if there are difficulties," he said.

Roth said the Swiss franc tended to exaggerate currency moves compared with other European currencies. This was an argument for maintaining Swiss monetary independence from other European countries, although the economies are closely linked.
At the same time, however, Swiss monetary policy should aim for price stability, he said, emphasising that structural changes were needed as well.
"Only if Switzerland is capable of preserving and at the same time augmenting its advantages will it be able to find a lasting way to growth, and be able to reabsorb its unemployed.

"This will demand of it not only favourable monetary conditions -- long-run price stability -- but also profound structural adjustments, and beyond that, perhaps a new way of doing business," Roth said.
